lessons.title: Short-Term vs Long-Term: Holding Periods Across Asset Classes

body.text: The same gain can be taxed at 20%, at 12.5%, at your slab rate or not at all. Very often, the only thing that decides which is how long you held the asset.

children.text: Karthik, a 31-year-old software engineer in Bengaluru, bought Nippon India ETF Nifty BeES on 20 August 2025 and sold on 11 August 2026 with a ₹90,000 gain. He needed the money for a bike down payment. Had he waited just 10 more days, that gain would have been long-term and, with no other long-term equity gains that year, fully covered by the ₹1.25 lakh annual exemption. Instead he paid 20% short-term tax plus 4% cess: ₹18,720.

body.label: Cost of Selling 10 Days Early
body.context: Tax on a ₹90,000 short-term gain on an equity ETF at 20% plus 4% cess, versus ₹0 if the same gain had been long-term and within the ₹1.25 lakh yearly exemption (assuming no other long-term equity gains in the year and ignoring surcharge).

children.text: Why the Label Matters

markDefs.definition: A gain on transfer of a short-term capital asset, meaning an asset held for not more than the relevant holding period (12 or 24 months), or an asset deemed short-term by law.

A gain on transfer of a long-term capital asset, meaning an asset held for more than the relevant holding period. Taxed at 12.5% for most assets, without indexation, for transfers on or after 23 July 2024.

children.text: Every capital gain is either a
short-term capital gain (STCG)
or a
long-term capital gain (LTCG)

. The label decides the tax rate, whether an exemption applies and, as you will see in Chapter 5, how losses can be set off. Chapter 2 onwards covers the rates in detail. For now, here is the headline picture for tax year 2026-27.

stats.context: Shares, equity mutual funds and equity ETFs where STT is paid

children.text: The Two Clocks: 12 Months and 24 Months
Section 2(101) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (section 2(42A) of the 1961 Act) defines a short-term capital asset. For transfers on or after 23 July 2024, the whole system runs on just two clocks.
12-month clock:
listed securities and a few specified units. Held for more than 12 months means long-term.
24-month clock:
everything else. Held for more than 24 months means long-term.
No clock at all:
a few assets are deemed short-term whatever the holding period, under section 76 of the 2025 Act (section 50AA of the 1961 Act).

body.text: "More than" is not "equal to". An asset held for exactly 12 months (or exactly 24 months) is still short-term. If you bought Gold BeES on 20 August 2025, the safest long-term sale date is 21 August 2026 or later. Do not plan to the day unless you are sure how the dates will be counted.

For mutual funds, check the fund category on the factsheet, not the fund name. An equity-oriented fund needs at least 65% in Indian listed equity. A "specified mutual fund" is one with more than 65% in debt and money market instruments, or a fund of funds putting 65% or more into such funds. Anything in between, such as many multi-asset and gold funds of funds, sits on the 24-month clock.

body.title: Which Sale Is Long-Term?
body.question: Each asset below is sold today. Which one gives a long-term capital gain?
options: Gold BeES units bought on NSE 14 months ago
A flat in Pune registered 23 months ago
Unlisted shares of a Bengaluru startup bought 18 months ago
body.explanation: Gold BeES is a listed ETF, so it runs on the 12-month clock and 14 months makes it long-term. Jewellery, property and unlisted shares all need more than 24 months, so 20, 23 and 18 months are all still short-term. Same metal, different wrapper, different clock.

body.title: The Debt Fund Trap
body.textWithBlank: Units of a debt mutual fund bought on or after 1 April 2023 are treated as ___ capital assets, however long you hold them.
body.explanation: Section 76 of the 2025 Act (section 50AA of the 1961 Act) deems gains on these "specified mutual fund" units to be short-term, so they are added to your income and taxed at your slab rate. Chapter 3 covers this in detail.

children.text: How the Rules Got Here

events.title: Property clock cut to 24 months
events.description: Land and buildings moved from a 36-month to a 24-month holding period. Unlisted shares were already on 24 months.

events.title: Debt funds lose long-term status
events.description: Units of funds with not more than 35% in domestic equity, bought on or after this date, became deemed short-term regardless of holding period.

events.title: Two clocks only
events.description: Union Budget 2024 collapsed the system to 12 months for listed securities and 24 months for everything else. Gold, jewellery and debt funds bought earlier came down from 36 months. LTCG moved to a flat 12.5%.

events.title: Specified mutual fund redefined
events.description: The deemed short-term rule was narrowed to funds with more than 65% in debt and money market instruments, so gold funds, international funds and many hybrids moved back to normal 24-month treatment.

events.title: Income-tax Act, 2025 takes effect
events.description: Same two clocks, new section numbers: section 2(101) replaces 2(42A) and section 76 replaces 50AA. Budget 2026 made no change to holding periods.

Short-term gain taxed at slab rate

children.text: Counting the Months Correctly

The holding period runs from the date you acquire the asset to the date you transfer it. For shares and ETFs bought on a stock exchange, the date on your broker's contract note (the trade date) is taken as the date of purchase, and the contract note date on the sale is the date of transfer. This position comes from CBDT Circular No. 704 of 1995, extended to demat holdings by Circular No. 768 of 1998.

body.latex: \text{Holding Period} = \text{Date of Transfer} - \text{Date of Acquisition}\\[6pt]\text{Long-term} \iff \text{Holding Period} > 12 \text{ or } 24 \text{ months}
body.caption: Pick the 12-month or 24-month threshold from the asset table above. Deemed short-term assets skip this test altogether.

body.title: Count the Months
body.prompt: Sneha's flat in Navi Mumbai was registered in her name on 5 August 2024. She signs and registers the sale deed on 1 June 2026. How many complete months has she held the flat?
body.explanation: 5 August 2024 to 5 May 2026 is 21 complete months. The 22nd month would complete only on 5 June 2026, and she sells on 1 June. With 21 months against a 24-month clock, her gain is short-term and is taxed at her slab rate. Waiting until after 5 August 2026 would make it long-term and taxable at 12.5%.

body.title: Special Cases: Whose Clock Starts When?

content.caption: Common situations and how the holding period is counted

cells: Date of allotment of the bonus shares, not the date you bought the original shares
Date of allotment of the rights shares
The date the previous owner acquired the asset. Their holding period is added to yours
The date you acquired the original shares in the parent company
Bonds or debentures converted into shares
The date you acquired the original bonds or debentures
Mutual fund switch between schemes or plans
The switch date, because a switch is a fresh purchase of new units
Each lot has its own date. For demat holdings, the oldest lot is treated as sold first (FIFO)

children.text: Under-construction property is the trickiest case. Courts have often counted the holding period from the date of the allotment letter where it gives the buyer a real right in the flat, rather than from the date of possession or registration. Outcomes depend on the facts and the documents, so get professional advice before relying on an allotment date.

body.title: The Inherited Flat
body.scenario: Meera's father bought a flat in Chennai in 2009. He passed away in March 2025 and Meera inherited it. She sells the flat in September 2026, just 18 months after inheriting it.
body.prompt: Is Meera's gain short-term or long-term? Explain why.
body.modelAnswer: Long-term. Inheritance is not a transfer, and for inherited assets the previous owner's holding period is included in Meera's. Her holding period effectively runs from 2009 to September 2026, far more than 24 months. The 18 months she held it personally does not matter on its own. Her cost will also be linked to her father's cost, which Lesson 3 covers.

children.text: Use the calculator above to try Karthik's case both ways. Enter the same ₹90,000 equity gain once as short-term and once as long-term and compare the tax. The calculator shows tax before the 4% health and education cess, so the short-term figure will read ₹18,000 rather than the ₹18,720 Karthik actually paid.

cards.definition: Held for not more than 12 or 24 months, as applicable, or deemed short-term by law. Section 2(101), 2025 Act (old 2(42A)).
Listed shares, equity-oriented fund units, listed ETFs, listed bonds, SGBs traded on the exchange, REIT and InvIT units, zero-coupon bonds.
Property, physical gold and jewellery, unlisted and foreign shares, non-equity non-debt funds and pre-April 2023 debt funds.
Always short-term regardless of holding: debt funds bought on or after 1 April 2023, unlisted bonds and debentures, market-linked debentures. Section 76, 2025 Act (old 50AA).
For exchange trades, the trade date on the broker's contract note marks both purchase and sale dates for counting the holding period.
First in, first out. For demat holdings bought in lots, the oldest shares are treated as sold first.

body.title: Before You Hit Sell: A Holding Period Check
steps: Identify the asset type and which clock it runs on: 12 months, 24 months or deemed short-term
For mutual funds, check the category and asset allocation on the latest factsheet, not just the fund name
Find the trade date on your contract note or the purchase date in your CAS for each lot
Remember FIFO: your oldest units are treated as sold first
For inherited or gifted assets, dig out the previous owner's purchase date
If you are within a few weeks of the long-term threshold, compare the tax both ways before selling

points: Short-term or long-term status decides the tax rate, exemptions and loss set-off, so check it before every sale
Listed securities and equity-oriented fund units become long-term after more than 12 months
Property, physical gold, unlisted and foreign shares and most other assets need more than 24 months
Debt funds bought on or after 1 April 2023, unlisted bonds and market-linked debentures are always short-term
An asset held for exactly 12 or 24 months is still short-term, because the law says "more than"
Gifted and inherited assets carry the previous owner's holding period, while bonus and rights shares start from allotment

Holding periods and rates reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 as in force for tax year 2026-27, with corresponding 1961 Act sections in brackets. Prices and examples are illustrative. Tax rules change with each Union Budget, so verify current provisions or consult a qualified tax professional before acting.
